metadata.title: SpaceX-Tesla: The directors negotiating the biggest merger ever

content.text:
SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) have entrusted five directors with the fate of the largest merger of all time, with the quintet hashing out the terms of a potential $3.5tn combination and racing to complete the deal before the end of the year.
Elon Musk's two public companies have appointed a handful of directors — three from Tesla and two from SpaceX — deemed financially "disinterested" to guide two special committees handling merger negotiations.
129.76 -3.59 (-2.69%)
As of 9:59:55 AM EST. Market Open.
Those directors are Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX and Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung from Tesla, according to people close to the process.
All five have longstanding ties to Musk and face a difficult task to map out how the two sprawling businesses could be brought together, win over shareholders and protect themselves from investor lawsuits that have plagued previous dealmaking by the billionaire's companies.
"They can't afford to let Elon bulldoze them. They need to do this by the book," one of the people said.
Special committees are standard practice for conflicted deals, but this process is unique with both sides sharing a chief executive, who is also the world's richest man.
The special committees have hired advisers — including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs for SpaceX and Evercore for Tesla — who are fine-tuning financial models that will form the basis for their negotiating positions in an all-stock merger, the people said.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. Botha declined to comment. Tesla, SpaceX and Evercore did not respond to written requests for comment.
The bankers are examining which parts of the proposed conglomerate overlap, such as AI models, chip-design efforts and data centres — while identifying complementary "synergies" that could include rockets, robotics and solar panels, the people said.
The two sides must then hammer out a fair "exchange ratio" for SpaceX and Tesla shares. This will be closely watched by institutional investors as well as Musk's army of retail shareholders, who hold an estimated 20 per cent of the electric vehicle maker and are very bullish on the company's valuation.
387.99 +2.53 (+0.66%)
As of 9:59:54 AM EST. Market Open.
"There is more friction than people assume. I don't think the committees are close yet," one of the people said. "But the culture of Elon's companies is to work 24 hours a day, seven days a week and then execute immediately."
"It could get done before the end of the year," they added.
If the financial terms can be settled, the companies will hash out governance rights and who takes crucial roles in the merged entity, including whether there is a chair, who will be chief financial officer and which directors will remain. "Elon will decide that and decide it quickly," said one person. "No one is under any illusions: this is his company."
Musk has complained about the special committee negotiations as an "odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can't be in the conversation". But a person close to the process said that it was "naive to think that this deal gets conceptualised, negotiated and executed without his input".
Under corporate governance rules in Texas, where both companies are incorporated, the special committees can consult with senior executives seeking information. But Musk cannot officially be involved in active negotiations. He has conveyed a message in public, saying that a combination was "a good idea" on a SpaceX earnings call last month.
The restrictions are far tighter on the Tesla side, where Musk controls only 20 per cent of the voting power, the people said. Tesla is also taking advice from Texan lawyers Joanna Lin and Wilson Chu at Dechert in Dallas. They advised a previous Tesla special committee on Musk's pay. Sullivan & Cromwell is advising Tesla on the corporate side.
SpaceX's lawyers are at Gibson Dunn and Vinson & Elkins is advising the its special committee, the people said. All the law firms did not provide official comments.
Tesla's annual meeting is on December 3, but approving the merger will probably require a separate extraordinary meeting. To win, Musk must secure more than 50 per cent of all possible votes, so any abstentions or absent ballots count as a "no".
If successful, the deal could give Musk majority control of a combined group. He controls about 84 per cent of the votes at SpaceX through super-voting shares, but only a fifth of Tesla, where each share carries one vote.
"This is not: 'let's merge the companies no matter what'. These require shareholder votes, which may or may not succeed, at least in the case of Tesla," Musk said at The New York Times' DealBook Summit last week.
"But even for my shareholder vote for SpaceX, I have to represent other shareholders," he added. "I can't just drag them into a non-economic merger that is bad for them because I'll obviously get sued."
The special committees will also have to walk through a legal minefield to get the deal done and ensure it can survive lawsuits and government scrutiny.
Some of the Tesla board were serving at the time of the SolarCity merger in 2016, which spawned years of painful lawsuits from angry shareholders who believed Musk improperly pursued the all-stock deal to bail out one of his other ventures.
The judge in the case eventually rejected the shareholder claims, but criticised Musk's close ties to the Tesla directors and his involvement in the negotiations.
Tesla then endured seven years of litigation in Delaware over Musk's historic $56bn pay package, which was twice voided by a judge but reinstated by the state's Supreme Court.
The difference in approach from Tesla and SpaceX so far is "striking", said one person involved. SpaceX is still a young public company and the person characterised their attitude as "the cult of Elon: we can do anything".
"But Tesla has been scarred by SolarCity, years of fights over his pay," the person said. "They know there will be lawsuits. Every text message and email will come out. So the directors are being super careful."
Adding to the drama, proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis last week advised shareholders not to re-elect chair Denholm, citing her failure to act on previous votes in favour of limiting directors to one-year terms and her oversight of Musk's pay.
Tesla's Chinese operations, which span manufacturing to a local version of its self-driving technology, could prove another significant issue, the people said. The Chinese government could balk at the deal, while the US might object given SpaceX's rocket technology and Starlink satellite business have national security implications.
Most likely, the carmaker will propose to ringfence them rather than sell, but all options are being discussed.
As such, the tie-up will also face antitrust scrutiny not only in the US but also in China, Europe and the UK. This could prove another stumbling block considering Musk's support for far-right political causes in both jurisdictions.
The deal will again put a spotlight on the boards' independence, which has been fought over in multiple lawsuits.
Other than the three committee members, the rest of Tesla's board — including Musk's brother, Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia and media scion James Murdoch — had to recuse themselves for being too close to Tesla's chief.
Longtime Musk investor Ira Ehrenpreis is ineligible because he sits on both boards. Antonio Gracias, head of Valor Equity Partners, was also a director at both, but stepped down from Tesla's board in 2021.
Additional reporting by George Hammond
